items.stem: Two coins are tossed. Let A be the event that the first coin shows head and B be the event that the second coin shows a tail. Two events A and B are
items.explanation: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. A occurs in HH and HT; B occurs in HT and TT. Their intersection has probability 1/4, equal to (1/2)(1/2), so they are independent. They can occur together, so they are not mutually exclusive; therefore none of the first three descriptions fits.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q1

items.stem: A card is drawn from a pack of 52 cards. If A = card is of diamond, B = card is an ace and A ∩ B = card is ace of diamond, then events A and B are
items.explanation: There are 13 diamonds, 4 aces and 1 card that is both. Since (13/52)(4/52)=1/52, the events are independent. Option A is correct; the printed key C is incorrect.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q2

items.stem: The probabilities of three mutually exclusive events are 2/3, 1/4 and 1/6. The statement is
items.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have a union probability equal to the sum of their probabilities. Here 2/3+1/4+1/6=13/12, which exceeds 1. Such events cannot exist, so the statement is false.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q3

items.stem: If P(A₁ ∪ A₂) = 1 − P(A₁ᶜ)P(A₂ᶜ), where c stands for complement, then the events A₁ and A₂ are
items.explanation: The union formula is P(A₁ ∪ A₂)=1−P(A₁ᶜ ∩ A₂ᶜ). Thus the given equality says P(A₁ᶜ ∩ A₂ᶜ)=P(A₁ᶜ)P(A₂ᶜ), so the complements, and hence the events, are independent. Option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q4

items.stem: If (1 − 3p)/2, (1 + 4p)/3 and (1 + p)/6 are the probabilities of three mutually exclusive and exhaustive events, then the set of all values of p is
items.explanation: Each probability must be nonnegative. The first gives p≤1/3, the second p≥−1/4, and the third p≥−1. Their sum is 1. The allowable set is [−1/4,1/3], option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q5

items.stem: The event A is independent of itself if and only if P(A) =
items.explanation: Independence of A with itself requires P(A∩A)=P(A)². Since A∩A=A, writing p=P(A) gives p=p², so p is 0 or 1. Option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q6

items.stem: If A and B are independent events and P(C) = 0, then
options: A, B and C are independent
items.explanation: An event C with probability zero has zero-probability intersection with every event. Each pair involving C therefore satisfies the independence product rule, and the triple intersection also has probability zero, equal to P(A)P(B)P(C) because P(C)=0. All listed independence claims hold.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q7

items.stem: The probability that an ordinary or a non-leap year has 53 Sundays, is
items.explanation: A non-leap year has 52 full weeks and one extra weekday. That weekday is equally likely to be any day, so it is Sunday with probability 1/7.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q8

items.stem: Three letters are to be sent to different persons and addresses on the three envelopes are also written. Without looking at the addresses, the probability that the letters go into the right envelope is equal to
items.explanation: There are 3! equally likely assignments of three letters to three envelopes, and only one assignment puts every letter correctly. The probability is 1/6.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q9

items.stem: The probability of getting head and tail alternately in three throws of a coin (or a throw of three coins), is
items.explanation: In three fair tosses, the alternating sequences are HTH and THT. They are 2 of the 8 equally likely sequences, giving 1/4.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q10

items.stem: In a lottery there were 90 tickets numbered 1 to 90. Five tickets were drawn at random. The probability that two of the tickets drawn numbers 15 and 89 is
items.explanation: Among 90 tickets, the probability that both specified tickets are among the five drawn is (5/90)(4/89)=2/801.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q11

items.stem: Two numbers are selected randomly from the set S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} without replacement one by one. The probability that minimum of the two numbers is less than 4 is
items.explanation: There are C(6,2)=15 unordered pairs. The complement of a minimum less than 4 is that both numbers lie in {4,5,6}, giving C(3,2)=3 pairs. The probability is 1−3/15=4/5, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q12

items.stem: Among 15 players, 8 are batsmen and 7 are bowlers. Find the probability that a team is chosen of 6 batsmen and 5 bowlers.
items.explanation: To form the specified 11-person team, choose 6 of the 8 batsmen and 5 of the 7 bowlers. Divide C(8,6)C(7,5) by the number C(15,11) of all 11-person teams.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q13

items.stem: The probability of obtaining sum 8 in a single throw of two dice
items.explanation: The outcomes summing to 8 are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2). Five of the 36 ordered dice outcomes work, so the probability is 5/36.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q14

items.stem: Three mangoes and three apples are in a box. If two fruits are chosen at random, the probability that one is a mango and the other is an apple is
items.explanation: There are 3×3=9 ways to choose one mango and one apple, out of C(6,2)=15 pairs. The probability is 9/15=3/5, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q15

items.stem: A card is drawn at random from a pack of 100 cards numbered 1 to 100. The probability of drawing a number which is a square is
items.explanation: The squares from 1 through 100 are 1², 2², …, 10², ten values. The probability is 10/100 = 1/10.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q16

items.stem: A bag contains 5 white, 7 black and 4 red balls. Three balls are drawn from the bag at random. The probability that all the three balls are white, is
items.explanation: The favorable selections are C(5,3)=10 all-white triples. There are C(16,3)=560 triples total, so the probability is 10/560=1/56.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q17

items.stem: Two dice are thrown together. The probability that at least one will show its digit 6 is
items.explanation: Neither die shows 6 with probability (5/6)²=25/36. The probability of at least one 6 is 1−25/36=11/36, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q18

items.stem: A pair of a dice thrown, if 5 appears on at least one of the dice, then the probability that the sum is 10 or greater is [MP PET 2001]
items.explanation: Given at least one die is 5, 3 of the 11 equally likely ordered outcomes have sum at least 10: (5,5), (5,6), and (6,5). The conditional probability is 3/11, option C; the printed key D is wrong.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q21

items.stem: Four boys and three girls stand in a queue for an interview, probability that they will alternate position is [UPSEAT 2002]
items.explanation: For four boys and three girls to alternate in a seven-person queue, the only possible pattern is BGBGBGB. Of the 7! equally likely gender orders, 4!3! satisfy it, so the probability is 4!3!/7!=1/35.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q22

items.stem: If two dice are thrown simultaneously then probability that 1 comes on first dice is [Rajasthan PET 2002]
items.explanation: The first die is equally likely to show any of its six faces. One face is 1, so the probability is 1/6.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q23

items.stem: Out of 30 consecutive numbers, 2 are chosen at random. The probability that their sum is odd, is
items.explanation: There are 15 evens and 15 odds among the 30 integers. An odd sum needs one of each: 225 favorable pairs out of C(30,2)=435, giving 15/29, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q24

items.stem: Three integers are chosen at random from the first 20 integers. The probability that their product is even, is [Kurukshetra CEE 2002]
items.explanation: Among 1, 2, …, 20 there are 10 odd numbers. The product is odd only if all three selected integers are odd, with probability C(10,3)/C(20,3) = 2/19. Therefore the product is even with probability 17/19.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q25

items.stem: Two dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the points on two dice will be 7, is [IIT 1974; MNR 1981, 91; Rajasthan PET 1995, 97, 2002; UPSEAT 2000]
items.explanation: The six ordered outcomes summing to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1). Thus the probability is 6/36.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q26

items.stem: A bag contains tickets numbered from 1 to 20. Two tickets are drawn. The probability that both the numbers are prime, is [AISSE 1981]
items.explanation: There are eight primes from 1 through 20. Drawing two without replacement, the probability both are prime is C(8,2)/C(20,2)=28/190=14/95.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q27

items.stem: In a single throw of two dice, the probability of getting more than 7 is
items.explanation: Sums greater than 7 are 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12, with 5+4+3+2+1=15 outcomes. So the probability is 15/36=5/12.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q28

items.stem: If two balanced dice are tossed once, the probability of the event that the sum of the integers coming on the upper sides of the two dice is 9 is
items.explanation: The ordered outcomes with sum 9 are (3,6), (4,5), (5,4) and (6,3). The probability is 4/36=1/9.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q29

items.stem: The probability of getting number 5 in throwing a die is [MP PET 1988]
items.explanation: A fair die has six equally likely faces and one face marked 5. The probability is 1/6.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q30

items.stem: The probability of getting a number greater than 2 in throwing a die is
items.explanation: The faces greater than 2 are 3, 4, 5 and 6, four of the six outcomes. The probability is 4/6=2/3.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q31

items.stem: The chance of throwing at least 9 in a single throw with two dice, is
items.explanation: Sums of at least 9 occur in 10 ordered outcomes: 4 ways to make 9, 3 to make 10, 2 to make 11 and 1 to make 12. Thus the probability is 10/36=5/18.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q32

items.stem: The probability that the three cards drawn from a pack of 52 cards are all red is [MP PET 1999]
items.explanation: The probability all three cards are red is C(26,3)/C(52,3)=(26×25×24)/(52×51×50)=2/17, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q33

items.stem: The probability of getting a total of 5 or 6 in a single throw of 2 dice is
items.explanation: Two dice have 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. A sum of 5 has 4 outcomes and a sum of 6 has 5, so the probability is 9/36 = 1/4, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q34

items.stem: If a committee of 3 is to be chosen from a group of 38 people of which you are a member. What is the probability that you will be on the committee
items.explanation: The committee has C(38,3) possible choices. To include you, choose the other two from the remaining 37, giving C(37,2)/C(38,3), option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q35

items.stem: The chance of getting a doublet with 2 dice is [Kurukshetra CEE 2002]
items.explanation: Two dice show a doublet in the six outcomes (1,1) through (6,6), out of 36 outcomes. The probability is 6/36 = 1/6, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q36

items.stem: A bag contains 3 white and 5 black balls. If one ball is drawn, then the probability that it is black, is
items.explanation: Five of the eight balls are black. One draw therefore gives probability 5/8, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q37

items.stem: Two dice are thrown together. The probability that sum of the two numbers will be a multiple of 4 is
items.explanation: Among 36 ordered dice outcomes, sums divisible by 4 are 4, 8 and 12. These occur 3, 5 and 1 ways, respectively, for 9/36 = 1/4, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q38

items.stem: The probability of happening of an impossible event i.e., P(∅) is
items.explanation: An impossible event has no outcomes, so its probability is zero, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q39

items.stem: For any event A [Rajasthan PET 1995]
items.explanation: An event and its complement partition the sample space. Their probabilities sum to 1, so option B is true.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q40

items.stem: A bag contains 3 red, 4 white and 5 black balls. Three balls are drawn at random. The probability of being their different colours is [Rajasthan PET 1999]
items.explanation: There are 3×4×5 choices of one ball of each colour out of C(12,3)=220 triples. The probability is 60/220=3/11, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q41

items.stem: Find the probability that the two digit number formed by digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is divisible by 4 (while repetition of digit is allowed) [UPSEAT 2002]
items.explanation: There are 5²=25 two-digit strings. The divisible-by-4 endings are 12, 24, 32, 44, and 52. Thus the probability is 1/5, not listed; option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q42

items.stem: If P(A)=0.65, P(B)=0.15, then P(A̅)+P(B̅)= [Pb. CET 1989; EAMCET 1988]
items.explanation: The complements are 1−0.65=0.35 and 1−0.15=0.85. Their sum is 1.20, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q43

items.stem: If four persons are chosen at random from a group of 3 men, 2 women and 4 children. Then the probability that exactly two of them are children, is [Kurukshetra CEE 1996; DCE 1999]
items.explanation: Choose two of the four children and two of the five nonchildren. The desired probability is C(4,2)C(5,2)/C(9,4) = 60/126 = 10/21, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q44

items.stem: A single letter is selected at random from the word “PROBABILITY”. The probability that the selected letter is a vowel is [MNR 1986; UPSEAT 2000]
items.explanation: PROBABILITY has 11 letters, of which O, A, and the two I's are vowels. The probability is 4/11, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q45

items.stem: The probability of three persons having the same date and month for the birthday is
items.explanation: Once the first birthday is fixed, each of the other two people independently has probability 1/365 of matching it. The probability is (1/365)², option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q46

items.stem: Out of 20 consecutive positive integers, two are chosen at random, the probability that their sum is odd is
items.explanation: There are 10 odds and 10 evens. The favorable pairs number 10×10, out of C(20,2)=190, so the probability is 10/19, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q47

items.stem: A and B play a game where each is asked to select a number from 1 to 25. If the two numbers match, both of them win a prize. The probability that they will not win a prize in a single trial is
items.explanation: For each first number, one of the 25 second numbers matches. The chance of no match is 1−1/25=24/25, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q48

items.stem: If E and F are events with P(E) ≤ P(F) and P(E ∩ F) > 0, then
options: Occurrence of E ⇒ occurrence of F
Occurrence of F ⇒ occurrence of E
Non-occurrence of E ⇒ non-occurrence of F
None of the above implications holds
items.explanation: The probability order and positive intersection do not force any of the three event implications. For example, with equally likely outcomes {1,2,3,4}, E = {1,2} and F = {1,3}: P(E) = P(F), their intersection is positive, but neither event contains the other, and Eᶜ = {3,4} is not contained in Fᶜ = {2,4}. Hence none of the implications must hold, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q49

items.stem: A single letter is selected at random from the word “KURUKSHETRA UNIVERSITY”; the probability that it is a vowel is
items.explanation: KURUKSHETRA has 11 letters and UNIVERSITY has 10, for 21 total. There are 4 vowels in each word, so the probability is 8/21, option C. The printed key A is wrong.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q50

items.stem: From the word “POSSESSIVE”, a letter is chosen at random. The probability of it to be S is
items.explanation: POSSESSIVE has 10 letters, including four S's. The probability of selecting S is 4/10, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q51

items.stem: Out of 40 consecutive natural numbers, two are chosen at random. Probability that the sum of the numbers is odd, is
items.explanation: Among 40 consecutive integers there are 20 odd and 20 even. A pair has odd sum exactly when it has one of each: 400 favorable pairs out of C(40,2)=780, giving 20/39, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q52

items.stem: Two dice are tossed. The probability that the total score is a prime number is
items.explanation: Prime sums possible with two dice are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. They occur 1+2+4+6+2 = 15 ways, so the probability is 15/36 = 5/12, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q53

items.stem: A lot consists of 12 good pencils, 6 with minor defects and 2 with major defects. A pencil is chosen at random. The probability that this pencil is not defective is
items.explanation: Only the 12 good pencils are nondefective, out of 12+6+2 = 20 pencils. The probability is 12/20 = 3/5, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q54

items.stem: 7 white balls and 3 black balls are placed in a row at random. The probability that no two black balls are adjacent is
items.explanation: Place the seven distinct white balls first; they create eight gaps, and choosing three gaps for the black balls prevents adjacency. Equivalently, among the C(10,3) black-position sets, C(8,3) work. The probability is 56/120 = 7/15, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q55

items.stem: Twenty children are standing in a line outside a ticket window at Appu Ghar in New Delhi. Ten of these children have a one-rupee coin each and the remaining 10 have a two-rupee coin each. The entry ticket is priced Re. 1. If all the arrangements of the 20 children are equally likely, the probability that the 10th will be the first to want change is (Assume that the cashier has no change to begin with)
items.explanation: If the first nine children do not need change, each pays Re. 1, leaving nine one-rupee coins with the cashier. The tenth child cannot be the first to need change. The probability is 0, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q56

items.stem: 4 five-rupee coins, 3 two-rupee coins and 2 one-rupee coins are stacked together in a column at random. The probability that the coins of the same denomination are consecutive is
items.explanation: Treat each denomination as a block. The three denomination blocks can be ordered in 3! ways and the coins within them in 4! × 3! × 2! ways. Dividing by the 9! total orders gives 1/210, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q57

items.stem: Two small squares on a chess board are chosen at random. Probability that they have a common side is
items.explanation: An 8×8 board has 8×7 horizontal and 8×7 vertical adjacent pairs, 112 total, out of C(64,2)=2016 pairs. The probability is 1/18, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q58

items.stem: There are n persons (n ≥ 3), among whom are A and B, who are made to stand in a row in random order. Probability that there is exactly one person between A and B is
items.explanation: For each of n−2 middle positions, A and B can occupy the adjacent positions in either order. The probability is 2(n−2)/(n(n−1)), option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q59

items.stem: If m rupee coins and n ten-paise coins are placed in a line, then the probability that the extreme coins are ten-paise coins is
items.explanation: The chance the first end is a ten-paise coin is n/(m+n); then the other end has chance (n−1)/(m+n−1). The product is n(n−1)/((m+n)(m+n−1)), option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q60

items.stem: Twelve balls are distributed among three boxes. The probability that the first box contains 3 balls is
items.explanation: The count in the first box is binomial with parameters 12 and 1/3. Its probability of being 3 is C(12,3)(1/3)³(2/3)⁹=(110/9)(2/3)¹⁰, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q61

items.stem: Six boys and six girls sit in a row. What is the probability that the boys and girls sit alternately
items.explanation: There are 12! seatings. Alternation allows 2 starting genders and 6! orders for each group, so 2(6!)²/12!=1/462, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q62

items.stem: Word 'UNIVERSITY' is arranged randomly. Then the probability that both 'I' does not come together, is
items.explanation: UNIVERSITY has 10 letters and two I's, giving 10!/2! arrangements. Together, the I's form a block with 9! arrangements. The probability they are apart is 1−9!/(10!/2!)=4/5, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q63

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. If tail appears on first four tosses, then the probability of head appearing on fifth toss equals [IIT 1998]
items.explanation: The fifth toss is independent of the first four. Whatever appeared earlier, a fair coin has probability 1/2 of showing head on the fifth toss. Option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q64

items.stem: A determinant is chosen at random. The set of all determinants of order 2 with elements 0 or 1 only. The probability that value of the determinant chosen is positive, is
items.explanation: For a binary matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], the determinant is ad−bc. It is positive when a=d=1 and b,c are not both 1: 3 of 16 matrices. The probability is 3/16, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q65

items.stem: Out of 13 applicants for a job, there are 5 women and 8 men. It is desired to select 2 persons for the job. The probability that at least one of the selected persons will be a woman is
items.explanation: There are C(13,2)=78 pairs, of which C(8,2)=28 are all men. The chance of at least one woman is 1−28/78=25/39, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q66

items.stem: Two numbers are selected at random from 1, 2, 3, …, 100 and are multiplied, then the probability correct to two places of decimals the product thus obtained is divisible by 3, is
items.explanation: Only pairs of nonmultiples of 3 yield a product not divisible by 3. Thus the probability is 1−C(67,2)/C(100,2)=0.5533…, which rounds to 0.55, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q67

items.stem: Five digit numbers are formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8. What is the probability that they have even digits at both the ends [Rajasthan PET 1999]
items.explanation: There are 7P5 five-digit numbers without repeated digits. To have even digits at both ends, choose and order two of the four even digits, then fill the middle three places from the five remaining digits: (4P2)(5P3)/(7P5)=2/7, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q68

items.stem: The corners of regular tetrahedrons are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4. Three tetrahedrons are tossed. The probability that the sum of upward corners will be 5 is
items.explanation: Each upward corner is uniform on {1,2,3,4}, so there are 4^3=64 triples. The positive integer solutions to x+y+z=5 number C(4,2)=6. The probability is 6/64=3/32, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q69

items.stem: In a college, 25% of the boys and 10% of the girls offer Mathematics. The girls constitute 60% of the total number of students. If a student is selected at random and is found to be studying Mathematics, the probability that the student is a girl, is [MP PET 2001]
items.explanation: Among 100 students, 60 are girls and 40 are boys. Mathematics students number 6 girls and 10 boys. Given that the selected student studies Mathematics, the chance of a girl is 6/(6+10)=3/8, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q71

items.stem: There are m persons sitting in a row. Two of them are selected at random. The probability that the two selected persons are not together, is
items.explanation: Of C(m,2) pairs, m−1 are adjacent. Hence the nonadjacent probability is [C(m,2)−(m−1)]/C(m,2)=1−2/m, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q72

items.stem: If the integers m and n are chosen at random between 1 and 100, then the probability that a number of the form 7^m + 7^n is divisible by 5 equals
items.explanation: The residues 7ᵏ mod 5 cycle through 2,4,3,1. Divisibility occurs for pairs (2,3),(3,2),(4,1),(1,4). Each residue occurs 25 times, so the probability is 4×25²/100²=1/4, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q73

items.stem: Cards are drawn one by one at random from a well shuffled full pack of 52 cards until two aces are obtained for the first time. If N is the number of cards drawn, then P_r[N = n], 2 ≤ n ≤ 50, is
items.explanation: Choose one ace position among the first n−1, fix an ace at n, and choose two later positions. The probability is (n−1)C(52−n,2)/C(52,4)=(n−1)(52−n)(51−n)/(50×49×17×13), option A. The printed key B is twice this value.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q74

items.stem: A locker can be opened by dialing a fixed three digit code (between 000 and 999). A stranger who does not know the code tries to open the locker by dialing three digits at random. The probability that the stranger succeeds at the kᵗʰ trial is
items.explanation: The three-digit code is one of 1000 equally likely codes, and a correct guess can occur only once. Every position k in a uniformly random ordering of the 1000 codes therefore has success probability 1/1000, which is not listed. Option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q75

items.stem: Seven white balls and three black balls are randomly placed in a row. The probability that no two black balls are adjacent equals
items.explanation: Choose the positions of the three black balls among the ten slots. For no two to touch, choose 3 of the 8 gaps/slots available after accounting for required white separators: C(8,3) placements. Thus C(8,3)/C(10,3)=7/15, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q76

items.stem: A committee consists of 9 experts taken from three institutions A, B and C, of which 2 are from A, 3 from B and 4 from C. If three experts resign, then the probability that they belong to different institutions is
items.explanation: There are C(9,3)=84 groups of three resigning experts. Choosing one from each institution gives 2×3×4=24 groups, so the probability is 2/7, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q77

items.stem: There are four machines and it is known that exactly two of them are faulty. They are tested, one by one, in a random order till both the faulty machines are identified. The probability that only two tests are needed is
items.explanation: Only two tests are needed exactly when the first two machines tested are the two faulty ones. The two faulty positions are a uniform pair among C(4,2)=6 position pairs, so the probability is 1/6, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q78

items.stem: A five digit number is formed by writing the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in a random order without repetitions. Then the probability that the number is divisible by 4 is
items.explanation: There are 5! permutations. The divisible-by-4 endings are 12, 24, 32, and 52; each allows 3! arrangements of the remaining digits. The probability is 4×3!/5!=1/5, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q79

items.stem: Five persons entered the lift cabin on the ground floor of an 8-floor house. Suppose that each of them independently and with equal probability can leave the cabin at any floor beginning with the first. The probability of all five leaving at different floors is
items.explanation: Each person independently chooses one of 7 floors, giving 7^5 assignments. Distinct floors can be assigned in 7P5 ways. The probability is 7P5/7^5, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q80

items.stem: If A and B are two events, then the value of the determinant chosen at random from all the determinants of order 2 with entries 0 or 1 only is positive or negative respectively. Then
items.explanation: Of 16 binary 2×2 matrices, 3 determinants are positive and 3 negative, so P(A)=P(B)=3/16. Both inequalities A and B hold, while C is false; no unique A–C choice applies, so D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q81

items.stem: x_1, x_2, x_3, ..., x_50 are fifty real numbers such that x_r < x_(r+1) for r = 1, 2, 3, ..., 49. Five numbers out of these are picked up at random. The probability that the five numbers have x_20 as the middle number is
items.explanation: For x₂₀ to be the median of five selected values, choose two of x₁, …, x₁₉ and two of x₂₁, …, x₅₀. This gives C(19,2)·C(30,2) favourable selections out of C(50,5), option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q82

items.stem: A card is drawn from a pack. The card is replaced and the pack is reshuffled. If this is done six times, the probability that 2 hearts, 2 diamonds and 2 black cards are drawn is
items.explanation: In each draw, the probabilities are 1/4 for hearts, 1/4 for diamonds, and 1/2 for black cards. The multinomial probability of two of each is 6!/(2!2!2!)×(1/4)²×(1/4)²×(1/2)²=90/2¹⁰, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q83

items.stem: An even number of cards is drawn from a pack of 52 cards. The probability that half of these cards will be red and the other half black is
items.explanation: For each j=1,…,26, choose j red and j black cards. Vandermonde's identity gives ΣC(26,j)²=C(52,26), and exclude j=0 to get C(52,26)−1 favorable subsets. There are 2⁵¹−1 nonempty even-sized subsets, so option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q84

items.stem: Two numbers a and b are chosen at random from the set {1, 2, 3, …, 3n}; the probability that a² − b² is divisible by 3 is
items.explanation: The difference a²−b² is divisible by 3 when a and b are both multiples of 3 or both nonmultiples. For distinct numbers, the probability is [C(n,2)+C(2n,2)]/C(3n,2)=(5n−3)/(3(3n−1)), option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q85

items.stem: The probability that the birthdays of six different persons will fall in exactly two calendar months is
items.explanation: Choose the two represented months in C(12,2) ways and assign six birthdays to both with 2⁶−2 assignments. Divide by 12⁶ total assignments: C(12,2)(2⁶−2)/12⁶=341/12⁵, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q86

items.stem: A bag contains n white and n red balls. Pairs of balls are drawn without replacement until the bag is empty. The probability of each pair consisting of balls of different colours is
items.explanation: In each of the n pairs, one ball of each colour must occur. Choose which of the two orders (white-black or black-white) occurs in each pair, giving 2^n colour sequences. The total number of equally likely colour sequences with n balls of each colour is C(2n,n), so the probability is 2^n/C(2n,n), option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q87

items.stem: To avoid detection at customs, a traveller has placed six narcotic tablets in a bottle containing nine vitamin pills that are similar in appearance. If the customs official selects three of the tablets at random for analysis, the probability that the traveller will be arrested for illegal possession of narcotics is
items.explanation: The traveller is caught if the sample contains at least one narcotic tablet. The chance of selecting only vitamins is C(9,3)/C(15,3)=84/455. Its complement is 371/455=53/65, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q88

items.stem: Six different balls are put in three different boxes, no box being empty. The probability of putting balls in the boxes in equal numbers is
items.explanation: Condition on no box being empty. The 3⁶ assignments of six distinct balls to three labeled boxes, with empty boxes excluded, number 3⁶−3·2⁶+3=540. Equal occupancy has 6!/(2!)³=90 assignments, so the conditional probability is 90/540=1/6, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q89

items.stem: A man and a woman appear in an interview for two vacancies in the same post. The probability of man's selection is 1/4 and that of woman's selection is 1/3. What is the probability that none of them will be selected?
items.explanation: Assuming the two candidates' selection outcomes are independent, the chance neither is selected is (1−1/4)(1−1/3)=(3/4)(2/3)=1/2, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q90

items.stem: Three six faced unbiased dice are thrown together. The probability that exactly two of the three numbers are equal is
items.explanation: Choose the value appearing twice (6 ways), the different value (5 ways), and the position of the different die (3 ways). There are 90 favorable outcomes among 6^3=216, giving 5/12, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q91

items.stem: If the papers of 4 students can be checked by any one of the seven teachers, then the probability that all the four papers are checked by exactly two teachers is
items.explanation: There are C(7,2)(2⁴−2)=294 ways to assign the four papers to exactly two of seven teachers, with both used. There are 7⁴=2401 assignments altogether. The probability 294/2401 is not listed, so option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q92

items.stem: A and B each throw a die. The probability that A's throw is not greater than B's is
items.explanation: Of 36 ordered dice pairs, 6 are ties. Among the remaining 30, half have A's throw smaller than B's. Thus P(A≤B)=(6+15)/36=7/12, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q98

items.stem: Let a die be loaded in such a way that even faces are twice as likely to occur as the odd faces. The probability that a prime number will show up when the die is tossed is
items.explanation: Give each odd face weight 1 and each even face weight 2. The total weight is 3+6=9. The prime faces 2, 3 and 5 have weights 2, 1 and 1, so the required probability is 4/9, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q100

items.stem: A special die with numbers 1,-1,2,-2,0 and 3 is thrown thrice. The probability that the total is zero is
items.explanation: There are 6^3=216 ordered triples. Enumerating the six possible values on each throw gives 25 triples whose sum is zero, so the probability is 25/216, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q101

items.stem: If four small squares are chosen at random on a chess board, the probability that they lie on a diagonal line is
items.explanation: For one diagonal direction, the board has diagonal lengths 4,5,6,7,8,7,6,5,4. The number of four-square subsets on a diagonal is twice the sum of C(length,4), which is 364. Divide by C(64,4)=635376 to get 13/22692, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q102

items.stem: A letter is taken at random out of each of the words CHOICE and CHANCE. The probability that they should be the same letter is
items.explanation: The words CHOICE and CHANCE have common letters C twice, H once, and E once. Matching letter occurrences across the two words give 2×2+1×1+1×1=6 favorable pairs out of 36, so the probability is 1/6, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q103

items.stem: Let X be a set containing n elements. If two subsets A and B of X are picked at random, the probability that A and B have the same number of elements is
items.explanation: For a fixed subset size k, there are C(n,k) choices for each subset, so matching sizes contribute C(n,k)^2 ordered pairs. Summing over k gives C(2n,n) by Vandermonde's identity; all ordered pairs number 4^n. Thus option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q104

items.stem: A four figure number is formed of the figures 1, 2, 3, 5 with no repetitions. The probability that the number is divisible by 5 is
items.explanation: There are 4! equally likely four-digit arrangements. Divisibility by 5 requires the last digit to be 5; the other three digits can be arranged in 3! ways. The probability is 3!/4!=1/4, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q105

items.stem: An elevator starts with m passengers and stops at n floors (m ≤ n). The probability that no two passengers alight at the same floor is
items.explanation: There are nᵐ assignments of m passengers to n floors. Assignments with no shared floor number n(n−1)…(n−m+1)=nPₘ. The probability is nPₘ/nᵐ, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q106

items.stem: If ten objects are distributed at random among ten persons, the probability that at least one of them will not get anything is
items.explanation: There are 10¹⁰ equally likely assignments of ten objects to ten persons. Everyone gets an object only for a bijection, with 10! assignments. The probability at least one gets none is (10¹⁰−10!)/10¹⁰, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q107

items.stem: Cards are drawn one by one without replacement from a pack of 52 cards. The probability that 10 cards will precede the first ace is
items.explanation: The first ten cards must be non-aces and the eleventh an ace. The probability is (48/52)(47/51)…(39/43)(4/42)=164/4165, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q108

items.stem: Five different objects A1, A2, A3, A4, A5 are distributed randomly in 5 places marked 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. One arrangement is picked at random. The probability that in the selected arrangement, none of the object occupies the place corresponding to its number, is
items.explanation: There are 5! = 120 arrangements. Inclusion–exclusion gives D₅ = 5! − C(5,1)4! + C(5,2)3! − C(5,3)2! + C(5,4)1! − 1 = 44 derangements. Hence 44/120 = 11/30, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q109

items.stem: 4 gentlemen and 4 ladies take seats at random round a table. The probability that they are sitting alternately is
items.explanation: Fix the circular order of the four gentlemen in 3! ways. The four gaps between them must each hold one lady, arranged in 4! ways. Out of all 7! = 5040 circular arrangements, the probability is 3! × 4!/7! = 1/35, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q110

items.stem: Let x = 33^n. The index n is given a positive integral value at random. The probability that the value of x will have 3 in the units place is
items.explanation: The units digit of 33^n cycles 3,9,7,1 as n advances. It is 3 exactly when n is congruent to 1 modulo 4, which occurs in one of four equally frequent residues. The probability is 1/4, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q111

items.stem: There are 7 seats in a row. Three persons take seats at random. The probability that the middle seat is always occupied and no two persons are consecutive is
items.explanation: There are C(7,3)=35 equally likely sets of occupied seats. If seat 4 is occupied, seats 3 and 5 are forbidden for the other two people; among seats 1,2,6,7, four pairs are nonconsecutive. Thus the probability is 4/35, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q112

items.stem: The probability that out of 10 persons, all born in April, at least two have the same birthday is
items.explanation: The probability all ten birthdays are distinct is 30P₁₀/30¹⁰. Therefore the probability of at least one match is (30¹⁰−30P₁₀)/30¹⁰, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q114

items.stem: A and B draw two cards each, one after another, from a pack of well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. The probability that all the four cards drawn are of the same suit is
items.explanation: After the first card, the next three must match its suit. The probability is (12/51)(11/50)(10/49)=44/4165, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q115

items.stem: Three different numbers are selected at random from the set A = {1, 2, 3, ..., 10}. The probability that the product of two of the numbers is equal to the third is
items.explanation: There are C(10,3)=120 equally likely sets. A product relation with distinct entries requires the two smaller numbers to be 2 and 3, 2 and 4, or 2 and 5, producing 6, 8, or 10. Three sets qualify, so the probability is 3/120=1/40, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q116

items.stem: A point is selected at random from the interior of a circle. The probability that the point is closer to the centre than the boundary of the circle is
items.explanation: At distance r from the centre, the distance to the circle is R−r. Being closer to the centre means r<R−r, or r<R/2. The favorable area ratio is π(R/2)²/(πR²)=1/4, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q117

items.stem: Let A and B be two independent events. The probability that both A and B occur together is 1/6 and the probability that neither of them occurs is 1/3. The probability of occurrence of A is
items.explanation: Let the event probabilities be p and q. Independence gives pq=1/6. Also (1-p)(1-q)=1/3, so 1-p-q+pq=1/3 and p+q=5/6. The roots with sum 5/6 and product 1/6 are 1/2 and 1/3. Thus P(A) is either value, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q118

items.stem: For an event, odds against is 6 : 5. The probability that event does not occur is
items.explanation: Odds against are 6 unfavorable outcomes to 5 favorable outcomes. Hence the probability the event does not occur is 6/(6+5)=6/11, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q119

items.stem: An event has odds in favour 4 : 5, then the probability that event occurs, is
items.explanation: Odds in favour 4:5 give 4 favorable outcomes among 9 total. The probability is 4/9, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q120

items.stem: A card is drawn from a pack of 52 cards. A gambler bets that it is a spade or an ace. What are the odds against his winning this bet
items.explanation: There are 13 spades and 4 aces, but the ace of spades is in both groups, so 13+4-1=16 cards win. The other 36 cards lose. Odds against winning are 36:16=9:4, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q121

items.stem: The odds in favour of a certain event are 2 : 5 and odds against of another event are 5 : 6. If the events are independent, then the probability of happening of at least one of them is
items.explanation: The first event has probability 2/7. Odds against the second are 5:6, giving probability 6/11. Independence makes the probability neither occurs (5/7)(5/11)=25/77. Thus the probability at least one occurs is 1-25/77=52/77, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q122

items.stem: In a horse race the odds in favour of three horses are 1 : 2, 1 : 3 and 1 : 4. The probability that one of the horse will win with the race is
items.explanation: The three horses have win probabilities 1/3, 1/4 and 1/5 from their respective odds. Their win events are disjoint, so the probability one of these horses wins is 1/3+1/4+1/5=47/60, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q123

items.stem: Odds 8 to 5 against a person who is 40 years old living till he is 70 and 4 to 3 against another person now 50 till he will be 80. Probability that one of them will be alive next 30 years is
items.explanation: The survival probabilities are 5/13 and 3/7; the corresponding death probabilities are 8/13 and 4/7. Assuming independent lifetimes, exactly one survives with probability (5/13)(4/7)+(8/13)(3/7)=44/91, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q124

items.stem: One of the two events must occur. If the chance of one is 2/3 of the other, then odds in favour of the other are
items.explanation: The events are disjoint and one must occur. If one probability is 2/3 of the other's, their probabilities have ratio 2:3. The other's probability is 3/5, so its odds in favour are 3:2, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q125

items.stem: If a party of n persons sit at a round table, then the odds against two specified individuals sitting next to each other are
items.explanation: Fix one person's seat. The other has n-1 possible seats, of which 2 are adjacent. Thus the probability of adjacency is 2/(n-1), and the odds against it are (n-3):2, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q126

items.stem: If odds against solving a question by three students are 2 : 1, 5 : 2 and 5 : 3 respectively, then probability that the question is solved by only one student is
items.explanation: The success probabilities are 1/3, 2/7 and 3/8. By independence, exactly one succeeds with probability (1/3)(5/7)(5/8)+(2/3)(2/7)(5/8)+(2/3)(5/7)(3/8)=25/56, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q127

items.stem: Odds in favour of an event A are 2 to 1 and odds in favour of A ∪ B are 3 to 1. Consistent with this information the smallest and largest values for the probability of event B are given by
items.explanation: Odds in favour give P(A)=2/3 and P(A∪B)=3/4. Therefore P(B outside A)=1/12. Its minimum is 1/12 when B has no part inside A; its maximum is 1/12+2/3=3/4 when B contains all of A. Option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q128

items.stem: The chance of an event happening is the square of the chance of a second event but the odds against the first are the cube of the odds against the second. The chances of the events are
items.explanation: Let the second event have probability q; the first then has probability q squared. Equating the odds against gives (1-q squared)/(q squared)=((1-q)/q) cubed. The solution in the listed choices is q=1/3, so q squared=1/9. Option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q129

items.stem: If A and B are two mutually exclusive events, then P(A + B) =
items.explanation: For mutually exclusive events, P(A∩B)=0. The addition rule for a union is P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B), so it reduces to P(A)+P(B), option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q130

items.stem: If A and B are two events such that P(A ∪ B) + P(A ∩ B) = 7/8 and P(A) = 2P(B), then P(A) =
items.explanation: Since P(A union B)+P(A intersection B)=P(A)+P(B), we have 3P(B)=7/8 because P(A)=2P(B). Hence P(A)=2(7/24)=7/12, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q131

items.stem: A bag contains 5 brown and 4 white socks. A man pulls out two socks. The probability that these are of the same colour is
items.explanation: There are C(5,2)+C(4,2)=10+6=16 same-colour pairs among C(9,2)=36 pairs. The probability is 16/36=48/108, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q132

items.stem: The probability that a leap year will have 53 Fridays or 53 Saturdays is
items.explanation: A leap year has 52 full weeks and two consecutive extra weekdays. The extra pair includes Friday or Saturday for three possible starting weekdays out of seven. The probability is 3/7, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q133

items.stem: A box contains 10 good articles and 6 with defects. One article is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is either good or has a defect
items.explanation: Every chosen article is either good or defective, so the two categories cover all 16 articles. The probability of good or defective is 16/16=1, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q134

items.stem: The probabilities of occurrence of two events are respectively 0.21 and 0.49. The probability that both occurs simultaneously is 0.16. Then the probability that none of the two occurs is
items.explanation: P(A union B)=0.21+0.49-0.16=0.54. Therefore the probability neither occurs is 1-0.54=0.46, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q135

items.stem: A bag contains 30 balls numbered from 1 to 30, one ball is drawn randomly. The probability that number on the ball is multiple of 5 or 7 is
items.explanation: There are 6 multiples of 5 and 4 multiples of 7 from 1 to 30, with no overlap. Thus 10 of 30 numbers qualify, giving 1/3, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q136

items.stem: If P(A) = P(B) = x and P(A ∩ B) = P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ) = 1/3, then x =
items.explanation: P(A union B)=x+x-1/3=2x-1/3. Its complement is 4/3-2x, which is given as 1/3. Solving gives x=1/2, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q137

items.stem: A card is drawn from a well shuffled pack of cards. The probability of getting a queen of club or king of heart is
items.explanation: The queen of clubs and king of hearts are two distinct cards. The probability is 2/52=1/26, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q139

items.stem: If A and B are two independent events, then P(A + B) =
items.explanation: For independent events, P(A intersection B)=P(A)P(B). Substitution into the addition rule gives P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B), option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q140

items.stem: In two events P(A ∪ B) = 5/6, P(Aᶜ) = 5/6, P(B) = 2/3, then A and B are
items.explanation: P(A)=1-P(A complement)=1/6. Then P(A intersection B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A union B)=1/6+2/3-5/6=0. The events are mutually exclusive, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q141

items.stem: The probability that at least one of the events A and B occurs is 3/5. If A and B occur simultaneously with probability 1/5, then P(Aᶜ) + P(Bᶜ) is
items.explanation: P(A)+P(B)=P(A union B)+P(A intersection B)=3/5+1/5=4/5. Therefore P(A complement)+P(B complement)=2-4/5=6/5, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q142

items.stem: If A and B are arbitrary events, then
items.explanation: For any events, P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A intersection B), and P(A intersection B) is nonnegative. Thus P(A union B) is at most P(A)+P(B), option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q143

items.stem: If P(A) = 2/3, P(B) = 1/2 and P(A ∪ B) = 5/6 then events A and B are
options: Independent as well as mutually exhaustive
items.explanation: P(A intersection B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A union B)=2/3+1/2-5/6=1/3. This equals P(A)P(B)=(2/3)(1/2), so the events are independent, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q144

items.stem: A bag contains 5 black balls, 4 white balls and 3 red balls. If a ball is selected randomwise, the probability that it is a black or red ball is
items.explanation: The black and red categories are disjoint. There are 5+3=8 favourable balls out of 12, giving 8/12=2/3, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q145

items.stem: A card is drawn from a pack of cards. Find the probability that the card will be a queen or a heart
items.explanation: There are 4 queens and 13 hearts; the queen of hearts is counted in both groups. So 4+13-1=16 cards qualify out of 52, giving 4/13, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q146

items.stem: The chance of India winning toss is 3/4. If it wins the toss, then its chance of victory is 4/5 otherwise it is only 1/2. Then chance of India's victory is
items.explanation: By conditioning on the toss, the win probability is (3/4)(4/5)+(1/4)(1/2)=12/20+1/8=29/40, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q147

items.stem: Let A and B be events for which P(A) = x, P(B) = y, P(A ∩ B) = z, then P(Aᶜ ∩ B) equals
items.explanation: The part of B outside A has probability P(B)-P(A∩B)=y-z, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q148

items.stem: A and B are two events such that P(A) = 0.4, P(A ∪ B) = 0.7 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, then P(B) =
items.explanation: Use P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B). Thus 0.7=0.4+P(B)-0.2, so P(B)=0.5, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q149

items.stem: A card is drawn at random from a pack of cards. The probability of this card being a red or a queen is
items.explanation: There are 26 red cards and 4 queens, with 2 cards counted in both groups. The probability is (26+4-2)/52=7/13, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q150

items.stem: If P(A)=0.4, P(B)=x, P(A ∪ B)=0.7 and the events A and B are mutually exclusive, then x =
items.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B). Hence x=0.7-0.4=0.3=3/10, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q151

items.stem: One card is drawn randomly from a pack of 52 cards, then the probability that it is a king or spade is
items.explanation: There are 4 kings and 13 spades, with the king of spades counted twice. The probability is (4+13-1)/52=4/13, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q152

items.stem: The chance of throwing a total of 7 or 12 with 2 dice,
items.explanation: Two dice have 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. A total of 7 has 6 outcomes and a total of 12 has 1, giving 7/36, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q153

items.stem: The probabilities of three mutually exclusive events A, B and C are given by 2/3, 1/4 and 1/6 respectively. The statement
items.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have disjoint union, so their probabilities must sum to at most 1. Here 2/3+1/4+1/6=13/12>1; the statement is false, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q154

items.stem: If A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ are any n events, then
options: P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + … + P(Aₙ)
P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ) > P(A₁) + P(A₂) + … + P(Aₙ)
P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ) ≤ P(A₁) + P(A₂) + … + P(Aₙ)
items.explanation: The union bound gives P(⋃A_i)<=ΣP(A_i) for any events; equality needs disjointness. Option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q155

items.stem: In a class of 125 students 70 passed in Mathematics, 55 in Statistics and 30 in both. The probability that a student selected at random from the class, has passed in only one subject is
items.explanation: Only Mathematics is 70-30=40 and only Statistics is 55-30=25. Thus 65/125=13/25, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q156

items.stem: A speaks truth in 60% cases and B speaks truth in 70% cases. The probability that they will say the same thing while describing a single event is
items.explanation: They say the same thing if both are truthful or both are mistaken. The probability is 0.6*0.7+0.4*0.3=0.54, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q157

items.stem: The chances of throwing a total of 3 or 5 or 11 with two dice is
items.explanation: For two dice, totals 3, 5 and 11 have 2, 4 and 2 outcomes. Their disjoint union has 8/36=2/9 outcomes, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q158

items.stem: In a box there are 2 red, 3 black and 4 white balls. Out of these three balls are drawn together. The probability of these being of same colour is
items.explanation: There are C(9,3)=84 triples. All-black gives C(3,3)=1 and all-white gives C(4,3)=4; all-red is impossible. The probability is 5/84, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q159

items.stem: A card is drawn at random from a well shuffled pack of 52 cards. The probability of getting a two of heart or diamond is
items.explanation: There are two cards that are a two of hearts or a two of diamonds, out of 52 cards. The probability is 2/52=1/26, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q160

items.stem: A committee of five is to be chosen from a group of 9 people. The probability that a certain married couple will either serve together or not at all is
items.explanation: There are C(9,5)=126 committees. With the couple together there are C(7,3)=35; with neither there are C(7,5)=21. The probability is 56/126=4/9, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q161

items.stem: A and B toss a coin alternatively, the first to show a head being the winner. If A starts the game, the chance of his winning is
items.explanation: Let p be A's chance to win from A's turn. A wins now with probability 1/2; after two tails (probability 1/4) the game restarts at A's turn, so p=1/2+p/4=2/3, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q162

items.stem: If A and B are two events, then the probability of the event that at most one of A, B occurs, is
options: P(Aᶜ ∩ B) + P(A ∩ Bᶜ) + P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ)
items.explanation: The event that at most one occurs is the complement of A∩B, so its probability is 1-P(A∩B). The three displayed expressions each equal this quantity, so option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q163

items.stem: Three persons work independently on a problem. If the respective probabilities that they will solve it are 1/3, 1/4 and 1/5, then the probability that none can solve it
items.explanation: Independence makes the chance all three fail (2/3)(3/4)(4/5)=2/5, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q164

items.stem: The probability of hitting a target by three marksmen are 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4 respectively. The probability that one and only one of them will hit the target when they fire simultaneously, is
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q165

items.stem: If A speaks truth in 75% cases and B in 80% cases, then the probability that they contradict each other in stating the same statement, is
items.explanation: They contradict when A is truthful and B is not, or vice versa. The probability is (3/4)(1/5)+(1/4)(4/5)=7/20, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q166

items.stem: The probabilities that A and B will die within a year are p and q respectively, then the probability that only one of them will be alive at the end of the year is
items.explanation: Exactly one is alive when A dies and B survives, or A survives and B dies. The probability is p(1-q)+(1-p)q=p+q-2pq, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q167

items.stem: If from each of the three boxes containing 3 white and 1 black, 2 white and 2 black, 1 white and 3 black balls, one ball is drawn at random, then the probability that 2 white and 1 black ball will be drawn
items.explanation: With one draw from each box, exactly two whites can occur in three ways: (3/4)(1/2)(3/4)+(3/4)(1/2)(1/4)+(1/4)(1/2)(1/4)=13/32, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q168

items.stem: A student appears for tests I, II and III. The student is successful if he passes either in tests I and II or tests I and III. The probabilities of the student passing tests I, II, III are p, q and 1/2 respectively. If the probability that the student is successful is 1/2, then
statements: There are infinite values of p, q
items.explanation: Assuming the three test outcomes are independent, success is I intersect (II union III), with probability p(q+1/2-q/2)=p(1+q)/2. Setting this to 1/2 gives p=1/(1+q), so (p,q)=(1,0) is one solution and every q in [0,1] gives a solution. Statements (c) and (d) are true: CD.

A.why: If p=q=1, the student passes all tests, so success has probability 1, not 1/2.

B.why: Under independence, p=q=1/2 gives success probability (1/2)(1/2+1/2-1/4)=3/8.

C.why: p=1 and q=0 gives success probability 1*(0+1/2)=1/2.

D.why: For every q from 0 to 1, p=1/(1+q) is in [1/2,1] and makes p(1+q)/2=1/2.

items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q169

items.stem: A bag contains 3 white, 3 black and 2 red balls. One by one three balls are drawn without replacing them. The probability that the third ball is red, is
items.explanation: By symmetry of the draw positions, each of the 8 balls is equally likely to be in position three. Two are red, so the probability is 2/8=1/4, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q170

items.stem: The probability of A, B, C solving a problem are 1/3, 2/7, 3/8 respectively. If all the three try to solve the problem simultaneously, the probability that exactly one of them will solve it, is
items.explanation: Sum the disjoint cases where only one succeeds: (1/3)(5/7)(5/8)+(2/7)(2/3)(5/8)+(3/8)(2/3)(5/7)=75/168=25/56, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q171

items.stem: The two events A and B have probabilities 0.25 and 0.50 respectively. The probability that both A and B occur simultaneously is 0.14. The probability that neither A nor B occurs is
items.explanation: P(A union B)=0.25+0.50-0.14=0.61. Therefore P(neither)=1-0.61=0.39, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q172

items.stem: A basket contains 5 apples and 7 oranges and another basket contains 4 apples and 8 oranges. One fruit is picked out from each basket. Then the probability that the fruits are both apples or both oranges
items.explanation: The baskets are selected independently. Both fruits are apples with probability (5/12)(4/12)=20/144, and both are oranges with probability (7/12)(8/12)=56/144. Their disjoint cases total 76/144, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q173

items.stem: A, B, C are any three events. If P(S) denotes the probability of S happening, then P(A ∩ (B ∪ C)) =
items.explanation: Distribute A over the union. The result is the union of A intersect B and A intersect C. Inclusion-exclusion subtracts their overlap, A intersect B intersect C, giving option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q174

items.stem: If A and B are any two events, then the probability that exactly one of them occur is
items.explanation: Exactly one occurs in the disjoint cases A without B and B without A. Adding those probabilities gives P(A)+P(B)-2P(A intersect B), option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q175

items.stem: If A and B are any two events, then P(Aᶜ ∩ B) =
items.explanation: Split B into the disjoint parts inside A and outside A. Thus the probability of A-complement intersect B is P(B)-P(A intersect B), option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q176

items.stem: If A and B are any two events, then the true relation is
statements: P(A∩B) is not less than P(A)+P(B)−1
P(A∩B) is not greater than P(A)+P(B)
items.explanation: The intersection lower bound is P(A intersect B) at least P(A)+P(B)-1, so A holds. The intersection is contained in each event, so its probability is at most their sum, making B true. Inclusion-exclusion rearranges to C. The answer is ABC.

A.why: The general lower bound for an intersection is P(A)+P(B)-1.

B.why: An intersection is contained in A and in B, so it cannot exceed their sum.

D.why: Inclusion-exclusion subtracts the intersection; adding the union is not valid.

items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q177

items.stem: A bag contains 3 black and 4 white balls. Two balls are drawn one by one at random without replacement. The probability that the second drawn ball is white, is
items.explanation: By symmetry, either position is equally likely to contain any of the seven balls. Thus the second ball is white with probability 4/7, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q178

items.stem: If P(A)=0.25, P(B)=0.50 and P(A∩B)=0.14, then P(A∩Bᶜ) is equal to
items.explanation: The part of A outside B has probability 0.25-0.14=0.11. This is not among the first three options, so D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q179

items.stem: Suppose that A, B, C are events such that P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=1/4, P(A∩B)=P(C∩B)=0, P(A∩C)=1/8, then P(A+B) =
items.explanation: The union probability is 1/4+1/4-0=1/2. The printed notation A+B means the union, so option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q180

items.stem: For any two independent events E₁ and E₂, P{(E₁ ∪ E₂) ∩ (E₁ᶜ ∩ E₂ᶜ)} is
items.explanation: The first event requires at least one of E1 and E2; the second requires neither. Their intersection is empty and has probability zero, which is at most 1/4. Option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q181

items.stem: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a well-shuffled pack. Find the probability that one of them is an ace of heart.
items.explanation: The ace of hearts is the only target card. Its chance of appearing in two draws is 1-(51/52)(50/51)=2/52=1/26, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q182

items.stem: If P(A ∪ B) = 0.8 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3, then P(Aᶜ) + P(Bᶜ) =
items.explanation: The sum of the two marginal probabilities is P(A union B)+P(A intersect B)=0.8+0.3=1.1. The sum of their complements is 2-1.1=0.9, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q183

items.stem: If A and B are two independent events such that P(A) = 0.40, P(B) = 0.50, then P(neither A nor B) is equal to
items.explanation: Independence gives the probability of neither event as (1-0.40)(1-0.50)=0.30, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q185

items.stem: The probability of India winning a test match against West Indies is 1/2. Assuming independence from match to match, the probability that in a 5-match series India's second win occurs at the third test is
items.explanation: For the second win to occur at test 3, the first two results must contain exactly one win, and test 3 must be a win. There are two orders for the first two results, so the probability is 2(1/2)(1/2)(1/2)=1/4, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q186

items.stem: A box contains 3 white and 2 red balls. A ball is drawn and another ball is drawn without replacing the first ball, then the probability of second ball to be red is
items.explanation: By symmetry, the second draw is red with the same probability as the red share of the original box: 2/5, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q187

items.stem: The probability of solving a question by three students are 1/2, 1/4, 1/6 respectively. Probability of question is being solved will be
items.explanation: The probability that all three fail is (1/2)(3/4)(5/6)=5/16. So at least one solves it with probability 11/16=33/48, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q188

items.stem: Three groups of children contain respectively 3 girls and 1 boy, 2 girls and 2 boys, one girl and 3 boys. One child is selected at random from each group. The chance that the three selected consist of 1 girl and 2 boys, is
items.explanation: The selected children must be girl-boy-boy, girl-boy-boy, or boy-girl-boy. The probabilities are (3/4)(1/2)(3/4), (3/4)(1/2)(3/4), and (1/4)(1/2)(3/4), totaling 13/32, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q189

items.stem: A, B, C are three events for which P(A)=0.6, P(B)=0.4, P(C)=0.5, P(A ∪ B)=0.8, P(A ∩ C)=0.3 and P(A ∩ B ∩ C)=0.2. If P(A ∪ B ∪ C) ≥ 0.85 then the interval of values of P(B ∩ C) is
items.explanation: Let x be P(B intersect C). Since P(A union B)=0.8, adjoining C gives a total union of 1.2-x by inclusion-exclusion. Requiring this to be at least 0.85 gives x at most 0.35. The triple intersection is 0.2, so x is at least 0.2. The interval is [0.2,0.35], option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q190

items.stem: A student has to match three historical events—Dandi March, Quit India Movement and Mahatma Gandhi's assassination—with the years 1948, 1930 and 1942. The student has no knowledge of the correct answers and decides to match the events and years randomly. Let Eᵢ (0 ≤ i ≤ 3) denote the event that the student gets exactly i correct answers. Then
items.explanation: The six equally likely matchings give probabilities P(E0)=1/3, P(E1)=1/2, P(E2)=0 and P(E3)=1/6. Substitution verifies each of A, B, C and D, so the answer is ABCD.

A.why: The probabilities are 1/3+1/6=1/2, equal to P(E1).

C.why: E0 and E1 are disjoint, and P(E2)=0.

D.why: The three disjoint cases have probabilities 1/3+1/2+1/6=1.

items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q191

items.stem: Given that A, B and C are events such that P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=1/5, P(A ∩ B)=P(B ∩ C)=0 and P(A ∩ C)=1/10. The probability that at least one of the events A, B or C occurs is
items.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion gives the union probability 1/5+1/5+1/5-1/10=1/2. The triple intersection is zero because A intersect B is empty. Option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q192

items.stem: Suppose a die (with faces marked 1 to 6) is loaded in such a manner that for K = 1, 2, 3, …, 6, the probability of the face marked K turning up when the die is tossed is proportional to K. The probability of the event that the outcome of a toss of the die will be an even number is equal to
items.explanation: Weights proportional to face values are 1+2+3+4+5+6=21. The even faces carry weight 2+4+6=12, so the probability is 12/21=4/7, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q193

items.stem: An unbiased die is tossed until a number greater than 4 appears. The probability that an even number of tosses is needed is
items.explanation: A toss succeeds with probability 1/3 (a 5 or 6) and fails with probability 2/3. An even number of tosses means an odd number of failures followed by a success, with probability (2/3)(1/3) + (2/3)³(1/3) + … = (2/9)/(1 − 4/9) = 2/5, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q194

items.stem: For the three events A, B and C; P(exactly one of the events A or B occurs) = P(exactly one of the events B or C occurs) = P(exactly one of the events C or A occurs) = p and P(all the three events occur simultaneously) = p², where 0 < p < 1/2. Then the probability of at least one of the three events A, B and C occurring is
items.explanation: Adding the three pairwise exactly-one probabilities gives 2(S-T)=3p, where S is the sum of marginal probabilities and T the sum of pair intersections. Hence S-T=3p/2. Inclusion-exclusion adds the triple intersection p squared, giving (3p+2p squared)/2, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q195

items.stem: A man alternately tosses a coin and throws a dice beginning with the coin. The probability that he gets a head in the coin before he gets a 5 or 6 in the dice is
items.explanation: Let x be the chance of eventually seeing a head on a coin before a die shows 5 or 6. On the first coin, a head succeeds with chance 1/2. A tail followed by a die result below 5 (chance (1/2)(2/3)) restarts the same situation. Thus x=1/2+x/3, giving x=3/4, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q196

items.stem: Two cards are drawn successively with replacement from a pack of 52 cards. The probability of drawing two aces is
items.explanation: With replacement, each draw has ace probability 1/13 independently. The chance both are aces is 1/169, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q197

items.stem: A pack of cards contains 4 aces, 4 kings, 4 queens and 4 jacks. Two cards are drawn at random. The probability that at least one of these is an ace, is
items.explanation: There are 16 cards total, four aces and 12 non-aces. The complement probability is C(12,2)/C(16,2)=66/120, so at least one ace has probability 54/120=9/20, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q198

items.stem: From a pack of 52 cards, two cards are drawn one by one without replacement. The probability that first drawn card is king and second is queen, is
items.explanation: The draws are ordered and without replacement. The chance of a king first and a queen second is (4/52)(4/51)=4/663, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q199

items.stem: A problem in Mathematics is given to three students A, B, C and their respective probability of solving the problem is 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. Probability that the problem is solved is
items.explanation: All three students fail with probability (1/2)(2/3)(3/4)=1/4. Therefore the problem is solved with probability 3/4, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q201

items.stem: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. The probability that the coin shows the head and the die shows 6 is
items.explanation: The coin and die are independent, so P(head and six)=(1/2)(1/6)=1/12, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q202

items.stem: A coin is tossed until a head appears or until the coin has been tossed five times. If a head does not occur on the first two tosses, then the probability that the coin will be tossed 5 times is
items.explanation: Given the first two tosses were tails, toss five is reached if tosses three and four are tails. This has conditional probability 1/4, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q203

items.stem: A bag contains 5 white, 7 red and 8 black balls. If four balls are drawn one by one without replacement, what is the probability that all are white
items.explanation: Four white balls drawn without replacement have probability (5/20)(4/19)(3/18)(2/17)=5/4845=1/969, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q204

items.stem: A bag contains 19 tickets numbered from 1 to 19. A ticket is drawn and then another ticket is drawn without replacement. The probability that both the tickets will show even number, is
items.explanation: There are nine even tickets among 19. Drawing two without replacement gives (9/19)(8/18)=4/19, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q205

items.stem: If P(A)=1/2, P(B)=1/3 and P(A∩B)=1/4, then P(B|A)=
items.explanation: By the conditional probability formula, P(B given A)=P(A intersect B)/P(A)=(1/4)/(1/2)=1/2, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q207

items.stem: From a pack of 52 cards two are drawn with replacement. The probability that the first is a diamond and the second is a king is
items.explanation: Replacement makes the draws independent. The probabilities are 13/52 for a diamond and 4/52 for a king, whose product is 1/52, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q208

items.stem: The probability that a teacher will give an unannounced test during any class meeting is 1/5. If a student is absent twice, then the probability that the student will miss at least one test is
items.explanation: The chance of no test in either of two independent meetings is (4/5)^2. The complement is 1-16/25=9/25, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q209

items.stem: If E and F are independent events such that 0 < P(E) < 1 and 0 < P(F) < 1, then (a) E and the complement of F are independent; (b) the complements of E and F are independent; (c) P(E|F)+P(complement of E|F)=1; (d) All of these
options: E and the complement of F are independent
The complements of E and F are independent
items.explanation: Independence is preserved when either event is complemented, so A and B hold. Given F, the probabilities of E and its complement sum to one, so C holds too. Therefore D, all of these.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q210

items.stem: The probability of getting at least one tail in 4 throws of a coin is
items.explanation: Use the complement: the only way to have no tail is four heads, with probability 1/16. Thus at least one tail has probability 15/16, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q211

items.stem: A bag contains 4 white balls and 2 black balls. Another contains 3 white balls and 5 black balls. If one ball is drawn from each bag, then the probability that both are white, is
items.explanation: The independent draws are both white with probability (4/6)(3/8)=1/4=0.25, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q213

items.stem: A binary number is made up of 16 bits. The probability of an incorrect bit appearing is p and the errors in different bits are independent of one another. The probability of forming an incorrect number is
items.explanation: An incorrect number occurs when at least one of the 16 bits is wrong. The chance all bits are correct is (1-p)^16, so the answer is 1-(1-p)^16, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q214

items.stem: The probabilities of winning the race by two athletes A and B are 1/5 and 1/4. The probability of winning by neither of them, is
items.explanation: If the win events are independent, neither wins with probability (1-1/5)(1-1/4)=3/5, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q215

items.stem: Seven chits are numbered 1 to 7. Three are drawn one by one with replacement. The probability that the least number on any selected chit is 5, is
items.explanation: The minimum is 5 when all three draws are at least 5, but not all are at least 6. Its probability is (3/7)^3-(2/7)^3=19/343. None of the listed expressions equals this, so D. The printed key C is wrong.
