items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q216

items.stem: A box contains 100 tickets numbered 1, 2, ..., 100. Two tickets are chosen at random. It is given that the maximum number on the two chosen tickets is not more than 10. The minimum number on them is 5 with probability [IIT 1985]
items.explanation: Conditioning on both tickets being at most 10 leaves C(10,2)=45 pairs. For minimum 5, the other ticket can be 6 through 10, giving five pairs and probability 5/45=1/9, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q217

items.stem: There are 20 cards. 10 of these cards have the letter 'I' printed on them and the other 10 have the letter 'T' printed on them. If three cards are picked up at random and kept in the same order, the probability of making the word IIT is
items.explanation: The ordered chance of I,I,T is (10/20)(9/19)(10/18)=5/38, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q218

items.stem: Let A={2,3,4,...,20}. A number is chosen at random from the set A and it is found to be a prime number. The probability that it is more than 10 is
items.explanation: Among the primes in 2 through 20 there are eight; four exceed 10. Conditional on the number being prime, the probability is 4/8=1/2, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q219

items.stem: A number is chosen at random from the numbers 10 to 99. By seeing the number a man will laugh if product of the digits is 12. If he chooses three numbers with replacement then the probability that he will laugh at least once is
items.explanation: Exactly four of the 90 two-digit numbers have digit product 12. A single draw misses with probability 86/90=43/45. Across three draws, at least one laugh has probability 1-(43/45)^3, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q220

items.stem: The probability that a married man watches a certain T.V. show is 0.4 and the probability that a married woman watches the show is 0.5. The probability that a man watches the show, given that his wife does, is 0.7. Then the probability that a wife watches the show given that her husband does is
items.explanation: Bayes formula gives P(wife watches given husband watches)=0.7(0.5)/0.4=7/8, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q221

items.stem: A pair of fair dice is rolled together till a sum of either 5 or 7 is obtained. Then the probability that 5 comes before 7 is [IIT 1989]
items.explanation: Each roll has four outcomes summing to 5 and six summing to 7. Other sums only delay the decision, so the chance 5 appears first is 4/(4+6)=2/5, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q222

items.stem: A bag contains 3 red and 5 black balls and a second bag contains 6 red and 4 black balls. A ball is drawn from each bag. The probability that one is red and other is black, is
items.explanation: The unlike-color cases have probability (3/8)(4/10)+(5/8)(6/10)=21/40, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q223

items.stem: Two persons A and B take turns in throwing a pair of dice. The first person to throw 9 from both dice will be awarded the prize. If A throws first then the probability that B wins the game is
items.explanation: A wins on each turn with probability 1/9. B wins if A misses and B succeeds, allowing any number of two-turn cycles: (8/9)(1/9)/(1-(8/9)^2)=8/17, option B. The printed key A is wrong.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q224

items.stem: An anti-aircraft gun takes a maximum of four shots at an enemy plane moving away from it. The probability of hitting the plane at the first, second, third and fourth shot are 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 respectively. The probability that the gun hits the plane is
items.explanation: The miss probabilities multiply: 0.6(0.7)(0.8)(0.9)=0.3024. Thus the chance of at least one hit is 1-0.3024=0.6976, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q225

items.stem: If A and B are two events such that P(A | B) = P(A′ | B′) = p and P(B) = 0.05, then value of p so that P(B | A) = 0.5 is
items.explanation: Let P(A given B)=p and P(A-complement given B-complement)=p. Then P(A)=0.05p+0.95(1-p). Solving 0.05p/P(A)=0.5 gives p=0.95, option C.

items.stem: A die is rolled three times. Let E₁ denote the event of getting a number larger than the previous number each time and E₂ denote the event that the numbers form an increasing A.P., then
items.explanation: There are 20 strictly increasing triples from six die faces. Six of these form an increasing arithmetic progression, so P(E1)=20/216=5/54 and P(E2)=6/216=1/36. Since E2 is contained in E1, their intersection has probability 1/36 and P(E2 given E1)=6/20=3/10. Also P(E1)=(10/3)P(E2). All statements A through D hold; the printed key omits D.

A.why: Every strictly increasing triple is one possible result counted in E1, so E2, the subset with equal positive increments, cannot be more probable.

B.why: E2 is a subset of E1 and contains six of the 216 equally likely triples, so the intersection probability is 6/216=1/36.

C.why: There are six arithmetic progressions among 20 increasing triples, giving conditional probability 6/20=3/10.

D.why: P(E1)=20/216 and P(E2)=6/216, so their ratio is 20/6=10/3.

items.stem: A reputed coaching employed 8 professors in the staff. Their respective probabilities of remaining in employment for three years are 2/10, 3/10, 4/10, 5/10, 6/10, 7/10, 8/10, 9/10. The probability that after 3 years at least six of these still work in the coaching is
items.explanation: Enumerating which professors remain, using their eight distinct probabilities, gives the chance of at least six remaining as approximately 0.19, option B.

items.stem: For a biased die the probabilities for different faces to turn up are given below: Face: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Probability: 0.1, 0.32, 0.21, 0.15, 0.05, 0.17. The die is tossed and you are told that either face 1 or 2 has turned up. Then the probability that it is face 1, is [IIT 1981]
items.explanation: Condition on face 1 or 2: the probability of face 1 is 0.10/(0.10+0.32)=5/21, option A.

items.stem: A biased die is tossed and the respective probabilities for various faces to turn up are given below: Face: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Probability: 0.1, 0.24, 0.19, 0.18, 0.15, 0.14. If an even face has turned up, then the probability that it is face 2 or face 4, is [MNR 1992]
items.explanation: The even-face probability is 0.24+0.18+0.14=0.56. The chance it is 2 or 4 is 0.42/0.56=0.75, which is absent from the options; D is correct and the printed key C is wrong.

items.stem: A bag X contains 2 white and 3 black balls and another bag Y contains 4 white and 2 black balls. One bag is selected at random and a ball is drawn from it. Then the probability for the ball chosen to be white is
items.explanation: Choose each bag with probability 1/2. The white probability is (1/2)(2/5)+(1/2)(4/6)=8/15, option C.

items.stem: A man draws a card from a pack of 52 playing cards, replaces it and shuffles the pack. He continues this process until he gets a card of spade. The probability that he will fail the first two times is
items.explanation: A spade has probability 1/4 on each replacement draw. Failing twice has probability (3/4)^2=9/16, option A.

items.stem: For any two events A and B in a sample space [IIT 1991]
options: P(A | B) ≥ (P(A) + P(B) - 1)/P(B), P(B) ≠ 0 is always true
P(A ∩ B) = P(A) - P(A ∩ B̅) does not hold
P(A ∪ B) = 1 - P(A̅)P(B̅), if A and B are disjoint
items.explanation: The intersection lower bound gives P(A intersect B) at least P(A)+P(B)-1; dividing by positive P(B) proves A. The identity in B actually holds, and C is not generally true for disjoint events. Thus A only.

items.stem: Three groups A, B, C are competing for positions on the Board of Directors of a company. The probabilities of their winning are 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 respectively. If the group A wins, the probability of introducing a new product is 0.7 and the corresponding probabilities for group B and C are 0.6 and 0.5 respectively. The probability that the new product will be introduced, is [Roorkee 1994]
items.explanation: Average over the three possible winning groups: (0.5)(0.7)+(0.3)(0.6)+(0.2)(0.5)=0.63, option D.

items.stem: If E̅ and F̅ are the complementary events of events E and F respectively and if 0 < P(F) < 1, then
items.explanation: Given F, E and its complement partition the sample space, so their conditional probabilities sum to 1; the same partition holds given the complement of F. The mixed-condition sums in B and C need not equal 1.

A.why: True: E and the complement of E partition the conditioning event F.

B.why: False in general: the two terms condition on different events.

C.why: False in general: these mixed conditional probabilities need not sum to one.

D.why: True: E and the complement of E partition the conditioning event complement F.

items.stem: Let A, B, C be three mutually independent events. Consider the two statements S₁ and S₂: S₁: A and B ∪ C are independent; S₂: A and B ∩ C are independent. [IIT Screening 1994]
options: Both S₁ and S₂ are true
Neither S₁ nor S₂ is true
items.explanation: Mutual independence gives the product rule for the intersections of A with B, C, and B intersect C. Substitution into the union and intersection formulas shows that A is independent of both B union C and B intersect C. Both statements hold, so choose A.

items.stem: In a certain town, 40% of the people have brown hair, 25% have brown eyes and 15% have both brown hair and brown eyes. If a person selected at random from the town has brown hair, the probability that he also has brown eyes, is [MNR 1988]
items.explanation: Among people with brown hair, 15% have both brown hair and brown eyes out of the 40% with brown hair. Thus P(eyes | hair)=0.15/0.40=3/8, option B.

items.stem: Let 0 < P(A) < 1, 0 < P(B) < 1 and P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Then [IIT 1995]
items.explanation: Independence makes the complements independent, so the probability of both complements is the product of their probabilities; it also gives P(A given B)=P(A). The first statement is generally false, while the second would require an extra equality between unrelated probabilities. Therefore C and D are true.

A.why: False: independence gives P(B given A)=P(B), not P(B)-P(A).

B.why: False: the two complements are not disjoint; the claimed sum generally exceeds their union probability.

C.why: True: complements of independent events are independent.

D.why: True: independence gives P(A given B)=P(A).

items.stem: It has been found that if A and B play a game 12 times, A wins 6 times, B wins 4 times and they draw twice. A and B take part in a series of 3 games. The probability that they will win alternately is
items.explanation: A wins one game with probability 6/12=1/2 and B wins with probability 4/12=1/3. The alternating wins can be A-B-A or B-A-B, so the probability is (1/2)(1/3)(1/2)+(1/3)(1/2)(1/3)=5/36, option B. The printed key says none of these which is incorrect.

items.stem: Two dice are rolled one after the other. The probability that the number on the first is smaller than the number on the second is
items.explanation: There are 36 ordered outcomes when two dice are rolled. The first is smaller in 15 of them, so the probability is 15/36=5/12, option D.

items.stem: The two friends A and B have equal number of daughters. There are three cinema tickets which are to be distributed among the daughters of A and B. The probability of all the tickets go to daughters of A is 1/20. The number of daughters each of them have is
items.explanation: If each friend has n daughters, the probability that all three distinct tickets go to daughters of A is C(n,3)/C(2n,3). Setting this equal to 1/20 gives n=3, so option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q242

items.stem: A bag contains (2n + 1) coins. It is known that n of these have a head on both sides, whereas the remaining (n + 1) coins are fair. A coin is picked up at random from the bag and tossed. If the probability that the toss results in a head is 31/42, then the value of n is
items.explanation: A double-headed coin always gives a head, and a fair coin gives a head with probability 1/2. The mixture probability is [n+(n+1)/2]/(2n+1)=(3n+1)/(4n+2). Equating this to 31/42 yields n=10, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q243

items.stem: The letters of the word PROBABILITY are written down at random in a row. Let E₁ denote the event that two I's are together and E₂ denote the event that two B's are together, then
items.explanation: PROBABILITY has 11 letters, with two I letters and two B letters. Either repeated pair occupies adjacent positions in 10 of the 55 possible position pairs, giving probability 2/11; the two marginal probabilities are equal. Grouping both repeated pairs as blocks gives the joint probability 9!/(11!/4)=2/55. Inclusion-exclusion gives the union probability 2/11+2/11-2/55=18/55, and the conditional probability is (2/55)/(2/11)=1/5. All four statements are true; the printed key omits D.

A.why: True: both repeated-letter pairs have the same 10 adjacent position pairs among 55 pairs.

B.why: True: treating II and BB as blocks gives 9! favorable arrangements out of 11!/4 total arrangements, a ratio of 2/55.

items.stem: In an entrance test there are multiple choice questions. There are four possible answers to each question of which one is correct. The probability that a student knows the answer to a question is 90%. If he gets the correct answer to a question, then the probability that he was guessing, is
items.explanation: A student who knows the answer is correct with probability 0.9. A guess is correct with probability 1/4, so the joint probability of guessing and being correct is 0.1 times 1/4=1/40. The total chance of a correct answer is 0.9+1/40=37/40. The requested conditional probability is (1/40)/(37/40)=1/37, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q245

items.stem: Three urns contain 6 red, 4 black; 4 red, 6 black and 5 red, 5 black balls respectively. One of the urns is selected at random and a ball is drawn from it. If the ball drawn is red, the probability that it is drawn from the first urn is
items.explanation: The prior chance of choosing the first urn is 1/3 and its red-ball chance is 6/10. The total red probability is (1/3)(6/10)+(1/3)(4/10)+(1/3)(5/10)=1/2. Therefore the posterior chance of the first urn is (1/5)/(1/2)=2/5, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q246

items.stem: There are 3 bags, each containing 5 white balls and 3 black balls. Also there are 2 bags, each containing 2 white balls and 4 black balls. A white ball is drawn at random. The probability that this white ball is from a bag of the first group, is
items.explanation: The first group contributes 3 times 5/8 white-ball chances, and the second contributes 2 times 2/6. Conditional on drawing white, the first-group probability is (15/8)/(15/8+2/3)=45/61, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q247

items.stem: A card from a pack of 52 cards is lost. From the remaining cards of the pack, two cards are drawn and are found to be hearts. Find the probability of the missing card to be a heart
items.explanation: If the missing card is a heart, 12 hearts remain and the chance that both observed cards are hearts is C(12,2)/C(51,2). If it is not a heart, that chance is C(13,2)/C(51,2). Applying Bayes rule with prior heart probability 1/4 gives 11/50, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q248

items.stem: One bag contains four white balls and three black balls and a second bag contains three white balls and five black balls. One ball is drawn from the first bag and placed unseen in the second bag. The probability that a ball now drawn from second bag is black is
items.explanation: A white transfer occurs with probability 4/7, leaving 4 white and 5 black balls in the second bag. A black transfer occurs with probability 3/7, leaving 3 white and 6 black. The final black probability is (4/7)(5/9)+(3/7)(6/9)=38/63, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q249

items.stem: A real estate man has eight master keys to open several new homes. Only one master key will open any given house. If 40% of these homes are usually left unlocked, the probability that the real estate man can get into a specific home if he selects three master keys at random before leaving the office is
items.explanation: There is a 2/5 chance the home is unlocked. If it is locked, three of the eight keys are selected, so the correct key is among them with probability 3/8. Access probability is 2/5+(3/5)(3/8)=5/8, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q250

items.stem: A coin is tossed 3 times by 2 persons. What is the probability that both get equal number of heads
items.explanation: The two people head counts are independent Binomial(3,1/2) variables. The probability that they match is the sum of C(3,k) squared for k from 0 to 3, divided by 2 to the sixth power. This is 20/64=5/16, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q251

items.stem: A bag x contains 3 white balls and 2 black balls and another bag y contains 2 white balls and 4 black balls. A bag and a ball out of it are picked at random. The probability that the ball is white is
items.explanation: The bag is selected with probability 1/2. The total white-ball probability is (1/2)(3/5)+(1/2)(2/6)=7/15, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q252

items.stem: If a coin be tossed n times then probability that the head comes odd times is [Rajasthan PET 2002]
items.explanation: For n at least 1 fair coin tosses, pair each sequence with the sequence obtained by switching every head and tail. One sequence in each pair has an odd number of heads, so the probability is 1/2, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q254

items.stem: In a bolt factory, machines A, B and C manufacture respectively 25%, 35% and 40% of the total bolts. Of their output 5, 4 and 2 percent respectively are defective bolts. A bolt is drawn at random from the production. If the bolt drawn is found to be defective, the probability that it is manufactured by machine B is
items.explanation: The defective-output shares are 0.25 times 0.05=0.0125 for A, 0.35 times 0.04=0.014 for B, and 0.40 times 0.02=0.008 for C. B share of all defective bolts is 0.014/0.0345=28/69, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q255

items.stem: An insurance company insured 2000 scooter drivers, 4000 car drivers and 6000 truck drivers. The probability of an accident involving a scooter driver, car driver and a truck driver is 0.01, 0.03 and 0.15 respectively. One of the insured persons meets with an accident. What is the probability that he is a scooter driver?
items.explanation: The accident-weighted counts are 20 scooter drivers, 120 car drivers and 900 truck drivers. Given an accident, the scooter probability is 20/(20+120+900)=1/52, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q256

items.stem: From an urn containing 3 white and 5 black balls, 4 balls are transferred into an empty urn. From this urn a ball is drawn and is found to be white. The probability that out of the four balls transferred, 3 are white and 1 black is
items.explanation: Let K be the number of white balls among the four transferred. Given K=k, a white draw has probability k/4. Weighting by the hypergeometric counts C(3,k)C(5,4-k), the posterior chance that K=3 is [C(3,3)C(5,1) times 3] divided by the sum over k of k C(3,k)C(5,4-k), which is 15/105=1/7, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q257

items.stem: In a test, an examinee either guesses or copies or knows the answer to a multiple choice question with four choices. The probability that he makes a guess is 1/3 and the probability that he copies the answer is 1/6. The probability that he copies the answer correctly, given that he copied it, is 1/8. The probability that he knew the answer to the question, given that he correctly answered it, is
items.explanation: The prior chance he knows the answer is 1-1/3-1/6=1/2. Correct-response contributions are 1/2 from knowing, 1/12 from guessing, and (1/6)(1/8)=1/48 from copying. Thus the posterior probability of knowing is (1/2)/(1/2+1/12+1/48)=24/29, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q258

items.stem: A company manufactures T.Vs at two different plants A and B. Plant A produces 80% and B produces 20% of the total production. 85 out of 100 T.Vs produced at plant A meet the quality standards while 65 out of 100 T.Vs produced at plant B meet the quality standard. A T.V. produced by the company is selected at random and is not found of meeting the quality standard. The probability that selected T.V. was manufactured by the plant B is
items.explanation: A produces 80% of the sets and has a 15% nonstandard rate, contributing 0.12. B produces 20% and has a 35% nonstandard rate, contributing 0.07. Given a nonstandard set, the chance it came from B is 0.07/(0.12+0.07)=7/19, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q259

items.stem: A coin is tossed 3 times (OR Three coins are tossed all together). The probability of getting at least two heads is
items.explanation: Eight equally likely outcomes occur in three fair tosses. Four have at least two heads: HHT, HTH, THH and HHH. The probability is 4/8=1/2, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q260

items.explanation: Use the complement: the only sequence with no heads is TTT, with probability 1/8. Therefore the chance of at least one head is 1-1/8=7/8, option A.

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed n time. If the probability that head occurs 6 times is equal to the probability that head occurs 8 times, then n is equal to [Kurukshetra CEE 1998; AMU 2000]
items.explanation: For a fair coin, the factors 2^(-n) cancel. Equal probabilities at 6 and 8 heads require C(n,6)=C(n,8). The coefficients match when n-6=8, giving n=14, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q262

items.stem: The mean and variance of a binomial distribution are 4 and 3 respectively, then the probability of getting exactly six successes in this distribution is
items.explanation: For a binomial variable, the mean is np=4 and variance is np(1-p)=3. Dividing gives 1-p=3/4, so p=1/4 and n=16. Thus P(X=6)=C(16,6)(1/4)^6(3/4)^10, option B.

items.stem: If X follows a binomial distribution with parameters n = 6 and p and 4P(X = 4) = P(X = 2), then p =
items.explanation: Using the binomial formula, 4P(X=4)=4*15*p^4*(1-p)^2 and P(X=2)=15*p^2*(1-p)^4. Canceling positive common factors gives 4p^2=(1-p)^2, so p=1/3, option D.

items.stem: The mean and variance of a binomial distribution are 6 and 4. The parameter n is [MP PET 2000]
items.explanation: For a binomial distribution, variance divided by mean is 1-p. Here 4/6=2/3, so p=1/3. Then np=6 gives n=18, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q266

items.stem: Suppose X follows a binomial distribution with parameters n and p, where 0 < p < 1. If P(X = r)/P(X = n − r) is independent of n and r, then
items.explanation: The binomial coefficient is the same in P(X=r) and P(X=n-r). Their ratio is (p/(1-p))^(2r-n). For this ratio not to vary with n or r, the base must be 1, so p=1/2, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q267

items.stem: If x denotes the number of sixes in four consecutive throws of a dice, then P(x = 4) is
items.explanation: Each of four independent die throws must be a six. The chance is (1/6)^4=1/1296, option A.

items.stem: The probability that an event will fail to happen is 0.95. The probability that the event will take place on 4 consecutive occasions is [Roorkee 1990]
items.explanation: Failure has probability 0.95, so success has probability 0.05. Four consecutive successes have probability (0.05)^4=0.00000625, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q269

items.stem: A die is thrown three times. Getting a 3 or a 6 is considered success. Then the probability of at least two successes is [DSSE 1981]
items.explanation: A success has probability 2/6=1/3. At least two successes in three trials has probability C(3,2)(1/3)^2(2/3)+(1/3)^3=7/27, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q270

items.stem: Let p be the probability of happening of an event and q its failure, then the total chance of r successes in n trials is [MP PET 1999]
items.explanation: Choose which r of the n trials succeed, then multiply the independent trial probabilities: C(n,r)*p^r*q^(n-r). This is option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q271

items.stem: In tossing 10 coins, the probability of getting exactly 5 heads is
items.explanation: There are C(10,5) ways to choose the five head positions among 2^10 equally likely outcomes. The probability is 252/1024=63/256, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q272

items.stem: Assuming that for a husband-wife couple the chances of their child being a boy or a girl are the same, the probability of their two children being a boy and a girl is
items.explanation: The two equally likely sequences with one boy and one girl are BG and GB. They are 2 of 4 outcomes, so the probability is 1/2, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q273

items.stem: Three coins are tossed together, then the probability of getting at least one head is [Rajasthan PET 2001]
items.explanation: Use the complement: the only outcome with no head is TTT, with probability 1/8. Thus the chance of at least one head is 1-1/8=7/8, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q275

items.stem: A die is tossed 5 times. Getting an odd number is considered a success. Then the variance of distribution of successes is [AIEEE 2002]
items.explanation: The number of odd results in five fair die throws is binomial with p=1/2. Its variance is np(1-p)=5/4, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q277

items.stem: An experiment succeeds twice as often as it fails. Find the probability that in 4 trials there will be at least three successes [AMU 1999]
items.explanation: Success occurs with probability 2/3. At least three successes in four trials has probability C(4,3)(2/3)^3(1/3)+(2/3)^4=16/27, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q279

items.stem: The records of a hospital show that 10% of the cases of a certain disease are fatal. If 6 patients are suffering from the disease, then the probability that only three will die is
items.explanation: The death count is binomial with n=6 and p=0.1. Exactly three deaths has probability C(6,3)(0.1)^3(0.9)^3=0.01458=1458*10^(-5), option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q280

items.stem: If the probabilities of boy and girl to be born are same, then in a 4 children family the probability of being at least one girl, is
items.explanation: The complement of at least one girl is four boys, with probability (1/2)^4. Therefore the required probability is 1-1/16=15/16, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q281

items.stem: A committee has to be made of 5 members from 6 men and 4 women. The probability that at least one woman is present in the committee, is
items.explanation: The complement is a committee of five men. Its probability is C(6,5)/C(10,5)=1/42. So the chance of at least one woman is 41/42, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q282

items.stem: A die is tossed thrice. A success is getting 1 or 6 on a toss. The mean and the variance of number of successes [AI CBSE]
items.explanation: Success on a throw has probability 2/6=1/3. For three throws, the mean is np=1 and variance is np(1-p)=2/3, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q283

items.stem: A coin is tossed 4 times. The probability that at least one head turns up is [MP PET 2000]
items.explanation: The complement of at least one head is four tails, with probability 1/16. The requested probability is 1-1/16=15/16, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q284

items.stem: If a die is thrown twice, the probability of occurrence of 4 at least once is [UPSEAT 2003]
items.explanation: The chance of no 4 in either throw is (5/6)^2=25/36. Taking the complement gives 11/36, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q285

items.stem: In a binomial distribution the probability of getting success is 1/4 and standard deviation is 3, its mean is [EAMCET 2002]
items.explanation: With p=1/4, the variance is np(1-p)=3n/16. A standard deviation of 3 means variance 9, so n=48 and the mean np=12, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q286

items.stem: If two coins are tossed 5 times, then the probability of getting 5 heads and 5 tails is [AMU 2002]
items.explanation: The five tosses of two coins give ten fair coin outcomes. Choosing the five positions for heads gives C(10,5)/2^10=63/256, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q287

items.stem: 6 ordinary dice are rolled. The probability that at least half of them will show at least 3 is
items.explanation: A die shows at least 3 with probability 4/6=2/3. Summing the binomial probabilities for 3 through 6 such results gives 656/729=41*2^4/3^6, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q288

items.stem: A fair die is tossed eight times. Probability that on the eighth throw a third six is observed is
items.explanation: For the third six to occur on throw eight, the first seven throws must contain exactly two sixes and the eighth must be a six. The probability is C(7,2)(5/6)^5(1/6)^3=C(7,2)*5^5/6^8, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q289

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed a fixed number of times. If the probability of getting seven heads is equal to that of getting nine heads, the probability of getting two heads is
items.explanation: For a fair coin, equality at 7 and 9 heads requires C(n,7)=C(n,9), which gives n=16. Then P(X=2)=C(16,2)/2^16=120/65536=15/2^13, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q290

items.stem: The probability that a candidate secures a seat in Engineering through "EAMCET" is 1/10. 7 candidates are selected at random from a centre. The probability that exactly two will get seats is
items.explanation: The seat count is binomial with n=7 and p=0.1. Exactly two successes has probability C(7,2)(0.1)^2(0.9)^5=21(0.1)^2(0.9)^5, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q291

items.stem: The probability that a man can hit a target is 3/4. He tries 5 times. The probability that he will hit the target at least three times [MNR 1994]
items.explanation: With hit probability 3/4, sum the cases of 3, 4 or 5 hits: C(5,3)(3/4)^3(1/4)^2+C(5,4)(3/4)^4(1/4)+(3/4)^5=459/512, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q292

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed 100 times. The probability of getting tails an odd number of times is
items.explanation: Pair every sequence of 100 tosses with the sequence obtained by changing the first toss. This switches odd and even tail counts, so each has probability 1/2, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q293

items.stem: A coin is tossed 7 times. Each time a man calls head. The probability that he wins the toss on more occasions is
items.explanation: Each call is a guess of head, so the number of correct calls in seven fair tosses is Binomial(7,1/2). By symmetry, the probability of more than 3.5 wins is 1/2, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q294

items.stem: A man draws a card from a pack of 52 cards and then replaces it. After shuffling the pack, he again draws a card. This he repeats a number of times. The probability that he will draw a heart for the first time in the third draw is
items.explanation: A heart has probability 1/4 on each draw, and replacement makes the draws independent. Missing twice and then drawing a heart has probability (3/4)^2(1/4)=9/64, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q295

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed n times. Let X be the number of times head is observed. If P(X = 4), P(X = 5) and P(X = 6) are in H.P., then n is equal to
items.explanation: For n tosses, cancel the common factor 2^(-n) in the three binomial probabilities. The harmonic condition becomes 2=(n-4)/5+6/(n-5), or n^2-19n+100=0. Its discriminant is -39, so none of the listed n values works: option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q296

items.stem: Five coins whose faces are marked 2, 3 are tossed. The chance of obtaining a total of 12 is
items.explanation: Starting with five 2s gives total 10. A total of 12 requires exactly two coins to show 3, which can happen in C(5,2)=10 of the 32 equally likely outcomes. The chance is 5/16, option D.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q297

items.stem: A coin is tossed 2n times. The chance that the number of times one gets head is not equal to the number of times one gets tail is [DCE 2002]
items.explanation: Equal numbers of heads and tails means exactly n heads in 2n tosses, with probability C(2n,n)/2^(2n). Its complement is the chance of unequal counts, matching option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q298

items.stem: A coin is tossed n times. The probability of getting head at least once is greater than 0.8, then the least value of n is [EAMCET 2003]
items.explanation: The chance of at least one head is 1-2^(-n). For n=2 this is 3/4, below 0.8; for n=3 it is 7/8, above 0.8. The least value is 3, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q299

items.stem: A box contains 24 identical balls, of which 12 are white and 12 are black. The balls are drawn at random from the box one at a time with replacement. The probability that a white ball is drawn for the 4th time on the 7th draw is [IIT Screening 1994]
items.explanation: For the fourth white to occur on draw seven, the first six draws must contain exactly three whites and draw seven must be white. The probability is C(6,3)/2^7=5/32, option C.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q300

items.stem: A die is tossed twice. Getting a number greater than 4 is considered a success. Then the variance of the probability distribution of the number of successes is
items.explanation: A success has probability 2/6=1/3. With two throws, the success count has variance np(1-p)=2(1/3)(2/3)=4/9, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q301

items.stem: In order to get at least once a head with probability at least 0.9, the number of times a coin needs to be tossed is
items.explanation: We need 1-2^(-n) to be at least 0.9. Three tosses give 7/8, which is too small; four give 15/16, so the least number is 4, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q302

items.stem: In a box of 10 electric bulbs, two are defective. Two bulbs are selected at random one after the other from the box. The first bulb after selection being put back in the box before making the second selection. The probability that both the bulbs are without defect is [MP PET 1987]
items.explanation: Each draw is good with probability 8/10, independently because the first bulb is replaced. Both are good with probability (8/10)^2=16/25, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q304

items.stem: A die is tossed thrice. If getting a four is considered a success, then the mean and variance of the probability distribution of the number of successes are
items.explanation: A four appears with probability 1/6. For three throws, the mean is np=1/2 and variance is np(1-p)=5/12, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q306

items.stem: Suppose A and B shoot independently until each hits his target. They have probabilities 3/5, 5/7 of hitting the targets at each shot. The probability that B will require more shots than A is
items.explanation: Let T_A and T_B be the first-hit times. Summing P(T_A=t)P(T_B>t) over t>=1 gives (3/5)(2/7)/(1-(2/5)(2/7))=6/31, which is option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q307

items.stem: In a precision bombing attack there is a 50% chance that any one bomb will strike the target. Two direct hits are required to destroy the target completely. The minimum number of bombs which should be dropped to give a 99% chance or better of completely destroying the target is
items.explanation: With n bombs, destruction means at least two hits, so the failure probability is (n+1)/2^n. At n=10 it is 11/1024, above 0.01; at n=11 it is 12/2048, below 0.01. The minimum is 11, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q309

items.stem: If the mean of a binomial distribution is 25, then its standard deviation lies in the interval given below
items.explanation: For a binomial variable with mean 25, variance is 25(1-p), which is at most 25. Thus the standard deviation is at most 5 and nonnegative; it lies in [0,5], option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q310

items.stem: If n integers taken at random are multiplied together, then the probability that the last digit of the product is 1, 3, 7 or 9 is
items.explanation: For the product to end in 1, 3, 7 or 9, every factor must have one of those four last digits. Each independent last digit has probability 4/10, so the result is (4/10)^n=2^n/5^n, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q311

items.stem: The probability of a bomb hitting a bridge is 1/2 and two direct hits are needed to destroy it. The least number of bombs required so that the probability of the bridge being destroyed is greater than 0.9, is
items.explanation: With n bombs, the chance of at least two hits is 1-(n+1)/2^n. At n=6 it is 57/64, below 0.9; at n=7 it is 120/128, above 0.9. The least number is 7, option B.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q314

items.stem: All the spades are taken out from a pack of cards. From these cards, cards are drawn one by one without replacement till the ace of spades comes. The probability that the ace comes in the 4th draw is
items.explanation: In a random ordering of the 13 spades, the ace of spades is equally likely to occupy any position. Its chance of being fourth is 1/13, option A.
items.ref: Probability assignment (315 question with answer), Q315
